utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Belinda Pidwell and Indah Susanti for the Prosecution today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, and Ms. Tatjana Savic appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And if there is nothing to detain us, may the usher please escort the witness back to the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, good morning to you. Again I give you the usual warning as to your solemn declaration before Mr. Zecevic begins his re-examination. Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Tusevljak. Mr. Tusevljak, at page 22493, the Thursday, your cross-examination, Ms. Korner read back to you a portion of the transcript from the Milosevic case; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You'll have to remind me because there's been a lot of talking since.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Korner read back to you a portion of the Milosevic transcript and conveyed to you one of the questions that you were asked during the Milosevic trial. "Sir" -- during your cross-examination in that case, that means. "Sir, do you remember between 1992 and 1995 any situation in which you carried out an investigation looking into war crimes against members of the SRK which you then passed on to the military prosecutor?" Your answer: "No, not in relation to war crimes, no." And then Ms. Korner went on to ask you if your answer at the time was accurate, which you confirmed. You remember that, sir, don't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you just please repeat your answer. You have to try and enunciate a bit more clearly because the answer reflects you saying no, in the negative.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the answer is yes. I did answer that to Ms. Korner at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, my question to you was: Do you remember this particular portion of your conversation or exchange with Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, during your chief and your cross you were shown that criminal reports against a person named (redacted) issued for a war crime committed in the Vogosca territory; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Was that back in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Was that crime -- that criminal report forwarded to the military prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: How is your answer from the Milosevic case to be understood, then, compared to what you are telling us now?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at the signature at the foot of that criminal report, you will see that it says Zivko Lazarevic, chief of the Vogosca Public Security Station. I was asked whether I did that myself and I said no, but quite obviously the Vogosca Public Security Station filed that criminal report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification, sir. At page 22494, the continuation of the previous exchange, you were asked this question by Ms. Korner. I'll need to read this in English in order not to have to back translate the LiveNote, and you will be receiving interpretation. [English] "All right. Now, the only question I'm putting to you at the moment - I'm going to come back to the book - is that the only war crimes that you actually spent any time investigating properly were those where Serbs were alleged to be the victims? So you either agree with that or you don't agree; that's all it requires." And your answer: "No. And I can give you some examples now. The reports against Jadranko Jeberovic [phoen]" - and it has a question mark - "for the murder of Bosniaks and Croats; a report of Predrag Djurovic, I believe that's what he was called, for raping a Bosniak woman." And further down: "That's what I can recall at the moment. These people weren't reported for war crimes, but they were reported for aggravated murder by the police station, not the centre but by the police stations." [Interpretation] Do you remember this portion of your conversation with Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You referred to these two specific cases: Jadranko, I think the last name was misrecorded, and Predrag Djurovic, these two specific cases; what were those in reference to?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were cases of aggravated murder on the one hand and rape on the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you personally produce either of these criminal reports?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the former.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say the former, which one do you have in mind specifically? Which person and what event?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jadranko Dilberovic, the murder of those two persons. My apologies, I can't follow the transcript over here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can the usher help because the witness cannot follow the transcript on his monitor, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, can you please slowly and articulately tell us the name of this reported person, the first name, then his last name, and where the crime occurred.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jadranko Dilberovic. The crime occurred at Grbavica. The Ministry of the Interior put this person into custody, and criminal charges were brought against this person for aggravated murder, Article 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And the victims were?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: One victim was a Muslim, Bosniak, and the other victim was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When did this crime occur?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe in May 1992, although it has been a long time and I can no longer be certain about the timing. I think it was right at the beginning of the war, meaning May.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At page 22502, you had another exchange with Ms. Korner about the number of perpetrators, systemisation, organisation of the centre, and such-like. Do you remember that, sir?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, if you remember, the Sarajevo Public Security Station, within the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, how many public security stations did it number back then?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, 22 public security stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Was there any substantial difference in terms of how each were organised between the Sarajevo Security Services Centre in the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Security Services Centre Sarajevo Romanija-Birac when it was part of the RS MUP?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of the organisation of the actual work and the actual posts, I don't think there were any differences. I think the previous model was simply copied.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What about the Sarajevo Romanija-Birac Security Services Centre of the RS MUP in terms of how it was organised, in terms of its organisational structure, did it include the Sarajevo SUP, the one that covered Sarajevo's municipalities that fell under the RS?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no Sarajevo SUP like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did that fact have any bearing whatsoever on the progress and co-ordination of public security stations throughout Sarajevo territory during the Sarajevo Romanija-Birac Security Services Centre's operation?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that due to the fact that the Sarajevo SUP within the Sarajevo Romanija-Birac Security Services Centre didn't exist our communication was more difficult when we worked with these urban public security stations simply because there was no one mediating and co-ordinating our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. At page 22537 you were asked the following question by Ms. Korner, again in English for the transcript: [In English] "Well, you see, it might be that I misunderstood the tenor of your evidence, Mr. Tusevljak, in which case I'll stop taking you through this rather tedious exercise of having a look at payrolls. You're not saying, are you, therefore, that no crime police were operating anywhere in a Serb-held territories in the Sarajevo area? "Yes"; that's your answer. "Yes, if you understand what I mean, if I understood the question correctly, some stations functioned and in some police station it didn't function at all." "Q. And you don't know one way or the other, do you, which police station it was functioning in and which it wasn't?" "A. Well, if you show me the list, I can tell you where operatives existed and where there were no operatives at all. "Q. Right. Well, have a look, please," at another document. [Interpretation] Ms. Korner never confronted you with that list following the exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, can the witness please be shown 65 ter 10138.8A.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you've seen this document before. It shows the structure of the Sarajevo Romanija-Birac Security Services Centre as it was in April through December 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Tab number?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, it's in the Prosecutor's binder. If you bear with me, I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's already helpful to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I'll ask you to use a pen --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have this on our screens. Thank you. Well, I'm informed that we are experiencing some problems with e-court, so perhaps we can return back to this a bit later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, does this mean that none of the documents can be shown to the witness at the moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, inasmuch as the witness has been using the binders with the hard copies rather than the screen, can't we proceed in that -- along that line?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm afraid, Your Honours, the witness has only a binder of Defence documents and I'm going to show -- the majority will be the Prosecutor's documents. But I don't think that the Prosecution has the documents in Serbian; that's the problem. In their binder, I guess, they have the English version of the documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: We do have them in both languages but we only have one copy of each, so if the witness is seeing them, I'm not seeing them in a direct reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pidwell, can't you see them on the screen? No?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I'm happy to follow them on the screen if they can come up, but I see we're having a problem already with one that's not coming up. But in my understanding it's only the witness who has a problem with the screen and not everybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pidwell, while we are waiting, does the Prosecution have a response on what Trial Chamber asked yesterday about the 12 translated documents?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: No, but I can consult with my learned friends who are listening and get back to you in the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Would it assist to give the witness the tab 58, the number that -- the chart that you were -- wanted?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We have it on the screen. Thank you very much. Will it be possible for a witness to mark on the screen on this document? Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I'm advised that we can try.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tusevljak, could you please mark for us the stations. But when you go about marking them, please say loud and clear which station you are marking. My question is: Mark the stations that had a crime prevention unit.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Should I mark just those that did, in other words?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Whichever way you like.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that case, I'll leave unmarked those that didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You pick whichever.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will pick those that did. I'll mark those that did. Ilidza, Novo Sarajevo, Zvornik, Ilijas, Vlasenica, Han Pijesak, Sokolac, Pale, Sekovici. Those are the ones that had the crime prevention units. And the remaining stations, they only had one when they were beginning to be set up, which is late in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Is that the same case for the whole period, April to September 1992, or even up until the end of 1992, when the service was formed in other stations as well?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in those other stations the crime prevention police began its formation from the end of September onwards, depending on the station.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let us just clarify once again: What was the main reason for this late establishment of services and departments for crime prevention in those public security stations?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly, the war. And then also there was manpower shortage. We did not have enough people who could carry out the tasks and duties of crime prevention inspectors.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the second day of your examination, page 21578 --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit 1D630. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, on page 21578, the topic was the timing of the conflict at Vrace. You said: It did not happen that night, it happened during the day on the 5th of April sometime in the afternoon, definitely afternoon. I was not at Vrace but I'm sure that it happened during the day and not during the night. "Q. ... right ... for whatever reason, Mr. Mihajlovic either put the wrong date deliberately or made a mistake."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's document 65 ter 20212, tab 62, Prosecution document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's a report on the work of public security station in Novo Sarajevo from the 1st of April until the 25th of December, 1992. It was drafted by Zoran Mihajlovic. In the first sentence we see: "Novo Sarajevo SJB was formed on the 5th of April ..." And you denied this. Ms. Korner then connected this to the situation at Vrace and in the end stated what I've just read out to you. Sir, take a look at the last page, who is the signatory of this document, page 4?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's signed by the chief of the public security station Novo Sarajevo, Zoran Mihajlovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: How many chiefs of the public security station Novo Sarajevo worked on that post from April until the moment Mr. Mihajlovic was appointed?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure, I think two or three.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In the document we looked at just now, we saw Milenko Jovanovic and Milanko Tepavcevic listed as chiefs of the public security station in Novo Sarajevo. Do you remember whether they were indeed on that post?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that after Tepavcevic, Mihajlovic was appointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember at which point in time Zoran Mihajlovic was appointed to chief of the public security station in Novo Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, towards the end of the year, the very end of the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to the previous two chiefs, Jovanovic and Tepavcevic? Where were they transferred?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jovanovic was seriously wounded at the school in Vrace, shot through both legs, and then he went for rehabilitation. After Tepavcevic left the post of chief, I believe he was transferred to the National Security Service or state security.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Where did Zoran Mihajlovic come from when he was appointed to the public security station?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He spent some time in the public security station in the crime prevention police. Then for about a month he was in the crime prevention police with me in Security Services Centre. And then from the chief -- from the post of the chief of crime prevention, he came to the post of the public security station, chief of the public security station.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the discussion about Sasa Blagojevic; and when was Blagojevic in the Security Services Centre Sarajevo Romanija-Birac; when he was not there, where he was; and such-like. You spoke about this topic on two occasion with Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, now I want to show you P1892.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, before we leave the document that's on the screen for the moment, can you give me the date of that document or can I have page 1 of the document again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I believe the date, Your Honours, is the 27th December, 1992. It's on the first page of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. You can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is an Official Note. Bijeljina, the 4th of August, 1992. It's a note on interviews which were conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's signed by the persons who drafted the note. Do you know any of the names listed here?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know all three of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What are they, those three individuals?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are the operatives. They are crime inspectors.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The middle one, the name that we find in the middle, who is he?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's Sasa Blagojevic, the one about whom we spoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to page 1. Did you learn anything about this? We see here that the official interviews were conducted with the persons listed here; they had been arrested in the area of Zvornik municipality as members of paramilitary formations. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not receive this Official Note. This had to do with the crime prevention administration. They were in charge of this. And we also see that the interviews were conducted in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Crime prevention administration of which CSB?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Crime prevention administration of the RS MUP, so not Security Services Centres but the headquarters of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Is that the same Sasa Blagojevic that we discussed before, the one that worked in Security Services Centre in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that he was in Zvornik at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The date is the 4th of August. Is that the time-period that you refer to when you say that he was in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have P997. It's tab 23, Defence document. Can we have the last page, please, it's page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is a report dated the 27th of August. Who submitted this report?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sasa Blagojevic, you can see it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Is this the same individual that you mentioned before, the one who worked in the Security Services Centre Sarajevo Romanija-Birac?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This document is dated the 27th of August and it's a report on the visit to the Vlasenica SJB. Are you aware of this report?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Was it sent to you or crime prevention police?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This report was made for the chief of the Security Services Centre and I was made aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 22621, Ms. Korner spoke about the hours, the total number of hours, spent on the investigation of the Golf vehicles, and on page 22621 she said: Are you going to agree with me, Mr. Tusevljak, that this operation had "a priority between ... July and the end of November in [sic] the Sarajevo CSB?" And your answer was: I'm not sure whether it had a priority or not, but if you look at the number of inspectors, you can see how many inspectors we had. Two white-collar crime inspectors worked on those matters. Do you remember this exchange with Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have 1D328. It's Defence document number 6. You can find it in your binder. It is Prosecution tab 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is the report on the meeting of heads of departments for criminality for the Romanija-Birac CSB. It details the meeting in Sokolac held on the 27th of July, 1992. Can you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You attended the meeting?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All the problems that you encountered in your work as well as the priorities you had, did you discuss this? Did you discuss the problems on this meeting?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the topic of the meeting, problems and ways of overcoming them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Was there any discussion about the priorities of the CSB?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so. I believe that some conclusions were drawn up at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Look at page 4, the last a sentence in the first paragraph, these are the words of Nikola Milanovic from the crime prevention administration of the headquarters of the MUP. Do you remember whether Nikola Milanovic spoke at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what he said on the meeting about the crimes committed by Serbs against civilian population?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember the details. It would be impossible. However, based on the content of my report, we can see briefly summarised who spoke about what.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Were there any conclusions made at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the very end of the meeting, we drew up conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can we find those conclusions in this report?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at the end of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Look at the conclusions and tell me whether any of them pertain to the priorities, and if so, what were the priorities in your work?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can read it out if you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, that is not necessary. They are contained in the document. I'm only interested in the conclusions relating to the priorities because the original question by Ms. Korner pertained to this topic. The document itself is in evidence; there is no reason to read it out loud.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the conclusions is that the communication should be improved, informing should be approved, a courier service should be established. Then we were supposed to receive requests for engagement of new personnel and proposals which had to be approved by SJB heads. Further on, we needed more forensic equipment because nobody had that. So we also requested that the problem of the judiciary should be solved because there were no judicial organs in the area of our centre. And at the end it says: Maximum engagement of all operational workers is requested for the tasks of documenting war crimes and submitting criminal reports against known and unknown perpetrators. And in relation to that: Maximum of the co-operation with the authorities in the areas where crime prevention services are carrying out their tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So in the operative sense, what was the priority based on these conclusions?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The operative priority was number 6, prevention of and documenting of war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, does any of the conclusions mentioned here mention the TAS factory and the thefts from that factory in Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, obviously not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Korner asked you about the property. Besides cars, were there any other objects of value stored in the TAS factory in Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name of the factory was UNIS Pretis. It's 15 kilometres long. 15.000 workers used to work there in a single shift. And then if you just think about the value of all the cars stored within the factory and you compare it with everything else that was within the perimeter of the factory, machinery, thousands of motors providing the power for the machinery, anything else you can imagine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was the owner of this factory, TAS UNIS Pretis in Vogosca, whatever the exact name was?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I suppose the state. It was state-owned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 22629, you were shown a document, P743, Prosecution binder 6A. You remember Ms. Korner showing you this document signed by Colonel Tomislav Sipcic, page 22629. You remember that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If you look at the header --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can pull the document up a little, please, so the witness can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It reads "Romanija Corps," then the date. On the right-hand side, "very urgent." Who is this document sent to or addressed to, this report?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Main Staff of the Republika Srpska BiH, that is, our own Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What about you at the Security Services Centre, did you ever receive reports from the Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At page 22638 there was some discussion regarding the situation at the Pale Public Security Station. You discussed problems that were occurring there at the time as well as the fact that Mr. Stjepan Micic spoke to you to complain about the situation that prevailed at the time in the public security station. You do remember that, sir, don't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Is it your recollection that before new people came into the leading positions, including the chief of the public security station, at Pale another member, high-ranking member, who worked at the station had been removed and charges had been brought against that person?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps remember that person's name?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe his first name was Vlajko, and I can't remember his last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps you can remember when this happened. Was it in 1992? And ultimately what was the whole thing about?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think a commission was set up by the RS MUP that was after Pale in 1992, including operatives from the Security Services Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. And the brief of that commission was? Was there a specific brief?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to establish any irregularities in the work of that particular police station. Based on that, when they went into the legal and administrative department, they established that there had been some irregularities there. The chief of that section faced criminal charges and all the other employees of that department were replaced or dismissed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now that we're on the subject - 22640 is the page - you were asked by Ms. Korner about members of the reserve police and active-duty police officers being disciplined. Ms. Korner goes on to say: "Mr. Tusevljak" -- just a minute, please. I'm going to try and find the exact reference and I'll read in English. [In English] "Now, I'm pointing out to you, Mr. Tusevljak, that from a case that you personally were involved in which on the face of it should have required disciplinary proceedings, shouldn't it? "A. Yes, but it wasn't up to me to start that, to trigger that. What I triggered was the start of investigation, but it wasn't up to me to propose any disciplinary steps or start disciplinary proceedings ... It was" -- And further down: "It was the responsibility of the chief to take the final decision on any steps to be taken."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Zecevic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You do remember that answer, don't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, in keeping with the regulations, did you have the authority to initiate disciplinary proceedings, and if so, in relation to whom?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had that power. I had the authority to initiate disciplinary proceedings only vis-à-vis employees who worked in my department within the Security Services Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday at page 22655, or, rather, 22709, there was mention there of some information shown to you by Ms. Korner, information put together by Kenan Delic, an inspector from the Sarajevo airport. And this was about the airport being taken by the JNA. This is 65 ter 20213, Prosecution tab 64. Do you remember that document, sir?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown page 3, the final paragraph of page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you commented at 22709 and you told Ms. Korner, having previously been asked whether you agreed that the JNA had taken the airport on the 5th of April: "Yes, but," you said; it says here that Kenan Delic's police were also at the airport at the police station up until the 12th of April. I don't think the answer that you provided was completely recorded at the time, therefore I wish to ask you a couple of additional questions in relation to this. Sir, in your opinion, based on Mr. Kenan Delic's report, when was it that the JNA took the airport in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This shows that members of the JNA arrived at the airport on the 6th of April. Nevertheless, within the airport itself there was the police station providing security. This shows clearly that the airport police station kept on operating until the 12th of April, 1992. It also shows Mr. Delic as saying that most of the police station's employees were operating in the area. So in practical terms, the JNA established control over the airport no sooner than the 12th of April, at least complete control.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. At page 22663 of yesterday's LiveNote, two persons bearing the same last name, Vlaco, were discussed. Do you remember that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We spent quite some time dealing with that. I'll just ask you two questions on this. What about Branko and Branislav; are these two names that are different names in the Serbian language? Are these two different names?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What would be a usual nickname for persons called either one of these two names?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Brane. That would be a perfectly ordinary and usual common nickname.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, you were shown yesterday a number of documents. P2369, which is the Vogosca -- Serb municipality of Vogosca bulletin, detention unit, Prosecution tab 28B. You remember being shown this document, sir, don't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this - I believe I asked you this already in chief, but just to be perfectly sure: Did you at the Security Services Centre ever receive bulletins such as this from the prison administration in Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we move on to the next document, please, P2368.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This bulletin is dated the 26th of July, 1992. Prison warden Branko Vlaco, and there is a list there. Sir, are you familiar with Mr. Branko Vlaco's signature?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown P2364, Prosecution tab 59.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Another document you were shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the Serbian, please. The original.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is the CV of Branislav Vlaco, something else you were shown by Ms. Korner. This document is signed by the person in question. Do you recognise this signature, the signature of Branislav Vlaco?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not familiar with that signature either.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As an experienced operative, and I know you are no expert in the field, but in your opinion what about these two signatures that we've just looked at, are the two different?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Back at university I took a course in graphology and handwriting analysis; that was part of the forensic subject that we were taught.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Would you like us to have the two documents side by side on your screen?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be nice, if possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have the two displayed side by side. P2368 on the right-hand side, we would like to see the original, tab 6A; we'd like to keep the Serbian and P2368 instead of English.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder whether this is really appropriate. The witness is not a handwriting expert. He is not proffered as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I was just going to ask Mr. Zecevic to pause so the Chamber can consult on the propriety of that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: No, Mr. Zecevic, the Chamber is of the view that the question that you were attempting to put would not be -- is not a question that could be properly put to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, with all due respect, my question was: "As an experienced operative, and I know you are no expert in the field, but in your opinion what about these two signatures that we have just looked at, are the two different?" And then the witness offered that he took a course in graphology and handwriting analysis and that is why I put both documents on the screen. But if Your Honours believe that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And the -- [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the president, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry. The difficulty is in your -- a part of your question was: Although you are not an expert, in your opinion ... which is the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honours. Anyhow, it's obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tusevljak --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please have 1D106. That is tab 1, Defence tab 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, the date is the 12th of July, 1992. This is a report by operatives of the Romanija-Birac CSB from Vogosca. They toured Vogosca on the 3rd of July, 1992. We've looked at this report already. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you also remember that the Security Services Centre was informed in this report and that the operatives established that there is no such thing as the crime service in -- or crime unit in Vogosca; they advised that one be established as soon as possible?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please go to page 2 of the document. At the end there is a list, a proposal was made and specific names proposed towards the bottom of that page. It says: We agree that a crime unit should be established and should comprise Brano Vlaco as a chief of the service, an employee of the station up to now and of the Security Services Centre in Sarajevo. We've heard everything that we have heard so far. Can you please tell me which Brane Vlaco is this a reference to? Is this about Branislav Vlaco or Branko Vlaco?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a reference to Branislav Vlaco.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You are concluding this based on what exactly?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Branislav Vlaco was an employee of the crime unit of the Sarajevo Security Services Centre, a white-collar crime inspector in that service.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say Sarajevo, do you mean before the clashes erupted in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I mean the period preceding the clashes in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have another topic to cover, a mere handful of documents, but I think this would be a convenient time for our break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pidwell, is the Prosecutor able to respond or give an answer to the question we put to you yesterday -- put to Ms. Korner yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In respect to the 12 documents which are remaining, we have received translations and reviewed them. I note that the documents were actually sought to be used with the witness who's currently on the stand and so it's a little bit problematic now that he's in re-examination. However, given we've reviewed them and in light of the comments that Your Honours made in your ruling about the other documents, we really take no position on these documents. We fail to see the relevance of at least half of them because they are outside of the indictment municipalities, but they are within the temporal time-frame of the indictment and we'll take our objection to their relevance as and when they're sought to be actually tendered by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So then we will add them -- we will allow Mr. Zecevic to add them to the 65 ter list. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, I received a suggestion from my colleagues. In order to round up your testimony, we again have 1D360 on our screens. It's the document that you marked at the very beginning of the session today relating to public security stations in which during 1992 there was a crime prevention administration. Sir, we are interested in the period between April and July, or perhaps end of summer, August, 1992. We can see from this document that nine stations had the crime prevention administration formed by the end of 1992. Would you be able to tell us or to write down on this document next to each of the marked stations how many operatives worked in each of them who were in charge of crime prevention in the aforementioned period? But first of all, could you repeat: How many people did you have directly under you in the Security Services Centre?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until July or August I had two and then four and then in November or December a slightly larger number of employees. You can see the exact numbers from the payrolls. I can now attempt to quote the numbers of the personnel in each police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Approximately.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. I can only give you an approximation because it's impossible for me to remember the exact numbers now. I believe that in Ilidza there were six operatives. In Novo Sarajevo, four. I am also including forensic technicians in these numbers. Then in Hadzici I think that until the end of the year there was only one or maybe even none.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Only mention those that had crime prevention service. And could you be so kind to only quote the number of the operatives, of inspectors. We are not interested in forensic technicians.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, then, here, instead of six I have to write five; and here, instead of four I have to write three.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Then cross out six and four, please.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for Zvornik, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Wait a minute, maybe it's better to erase this and then you can write the numbers again. So I'm only interested in the number of operatives, inspectors.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So five and three. I don't know for Zvornik. It wasn't our situation before 1992 so I can't remember. Ilijas, two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Shouldn't we, in respect of Zvornik, so that we don't confuse ourselves when we look back at this, put a question mark, having regard to his answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will you put a question mark on Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vlasenica I also don't know. Han Pijesak, one. Sokolac, one operative. Pale, three, I believe. And Sekovici, two.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you didn't know for Vlasenica. Could you put a question mark there.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the exhibit number for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So apparently it has to have a new marking, so ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit 1D631, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I hope we didn't lost it. [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, just one more thing before we move on to the last topic. On page 22466 of the transcript you were asked by Ms. Korner something about the document that you gave to the Stanisic Defence. She asked whether you gave them any documents before 2007; you said: No, as far as I know it was only after we started receiving formal requests. And then after this I showed you one such request and one document that you sent accompanied with the list of documents. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just for the transcript, and perhaps for some future use, did you act upon our requests in some other cases and send us documents?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever you contact the secretariat for relations with The Hague Tribunal, and I mean the secretariat within the government of the RS, and they forward your request to us, or in cases you contacted directly the Ministry of Interior of Republika Srpska, according to the law in co-operation with The Hague Tribunal of Republika Srpska all available documents are then sent to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps remember how many times you did that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I really wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But do you remember that it happened more than once?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Surely more than once.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the last topic. Document P160, tab 153 in the Defence binder. 153. It's a report about the meeting of the first collegium of the MUP of Republika Srpska held on the 1st of July. Ms. Korner asked you about this on page 22705. She quoted your own words from page --

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- 18, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but in e-court it's page 21 in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the same page in English; I believe it's one page before this one. It could be page 18 in English. 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Right, this is where you begin. Ms. Korner read out the last sentence in this paragraph, saying that at that meeting you said -- she was speaking to you, saying: You said that in Vlasenica out of 73 criminal reports, 23 were filed against Serbs. However, Ms. Korner, and I fully understand her, omitted to read the previous sentence. Could you read your words as they were recorded in this report, so that's one sentence before the last.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Tusevljak spoke about the lack of personnel engaged in criminal investigations at the Sarajevo Security Services Centre" --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, I probably wasn't clear enough. The last sentence in this paragraph begins with words "for example." I'm interested in the sentence immediately before this one. And you don't have to read it out loud. This is evidence.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Criminal reports are filed against everybody."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What did you have in mind when you said criminal reports are filed against everybody?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to the fact that the ethnicity of the perpetrator of criminal offence was irrelevant for us. We filed criminal reports against everybody who committed a criminal offence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 26 in e-court in Serbian and 23, I believe, in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in one of the conclusions. You were shown this conclusion by Ms. Korner. It's conclusion 6 relating to prevention and documenting of war crimes. However, she omitted, again, to show you conclusion 7. Could you comment on conclusion 7.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Should I read it out?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: There is no need for that. Just comment on it. What is it about? What kind of criminal offences are meant? When it says "serious crimes of endangering life," what is it about?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is about discovery of serious crimes such as looting, war profiteering, serious crimes against life and limb, and other criminal offences irrespective of who the perpetrators are.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just a short comment on the following: Serious crimes of endangering life, what exactly is this? What kind of criminal offences are we talking about here?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Aggravated murders.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, in conclusion 6 --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In English it's on the previous page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- we find the following: "Preventing and documenting war crimes and using all legally prescribed resources and methods for documenting such enemy activity ..." Ms. Korner read out this part. And then on page 22706, you stated: When you take a look at my discussion, you will see that I spoke about the crimes committed by Serbs. This conclusion relates only to the enemy activity in that sense, but nothing is specified about the enemy. What exactly does that word mean, who is it? There are some reports filed against known and unknown perpetrators. By that you mean to say that you had in your files reports filed against known and unknown perpetrators. And then Ms. Korner asked you: The Serbs in Bosnia and Republika Srpska considered their enemies those that you call Green Berets, HOS, Patriotic League, you considered them enemies? And you answered yes, "They were the enemy." Sir, could you explain whether in the Serbian language the word "enemy," in it's second declension, is it the same in plural and singular?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So when we find, as we find here, "enemy" as in "neprijatelje," is it possible to deduct from this whether it is plural or singular?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be both.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Generally speaking, whom did the Ministry of the Interior consider enemy?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perpetrators of criminal offences.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So we have the Green Berets here, the HOS, the Patriotic League, all these paramilitary organisations, in your opinion would this same group include some paramilitary units like the Yellow Wasps or groups like that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the group would include those two as our enemies during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, I will now show you 1D063, tab 290. You answered a question by Ms. Korner, also at 22706, saying that other instructions and orders had arrived from the Ministry of the Interior regarding war crimes. This is at page 22695. Just to make sure this is complete, the date on the document is the 19th of July. It is a document produced by the Ministry of Interior, signed by Mr. Stanisic, delivered to all Security Services Centres including the one in Sarajevo. Could you please read slowly paragraph 1 and paragraph 2 of these guide-lines or instructions being delivered to these addressees.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Proceeding in accordance with the conclusions adopted at the meeting of senior personnel on the 11th of July, 1992, whereby the tasks related to the discovery of documentation of war crimes or genocide and the submission of criminal reports, as well as in accordance with other enactments, (number strictly confidential 01-2/92 of the 16th of May, 1992) and orders were numbered among the priorities of the National Security Service and the crime prevention service, a questionnaire on war crimes and victims of genocide has been compiled in the information analysis administration. "A questionnaire will be completed at Security Services Centres for all persons regardless of ethnicity (Muslims, Croats, Serbs, and others) against whom criminal reports have been submitted on reasonable grounds for suspicion that they have committed the given crimes, as well as questionnaires for victims regardless of whether a criminal report has been submitted or the procedure of gathering evidence for the submission of a criminal report against the perpetrators is still in progress."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is the RZ form in relation to victims of war crimes. You see that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please comment on item 5 and item 6, or, rather, question 5 and question 6 of this form.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 5 is the victim's ethnicity. Number 6 is the victim's religion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, if Ms. Korner were right, if the position and the policy of the Ministry of the Interior had been to document war crimes but only those committed against Serbs, would there have been any need for a form like this to include this type of information?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There would have been no need at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, we talked in chief about the reasons that criminal offences committed in territory not under the control of the Ministry of the Interior of the RS were documented. You remember that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please remind us of that reason; why were you looking into that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would get contacted by citizens leaving the area. On their way out they would report those criminal offences to the local police stations and they would provide statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you document those statements and did you follow the statements up with specific criminal reports based on such documentation as you were able to obtain?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Based on this, we would forward reports to the competent prosecutors.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let us look at a number of criminal reports that you were shown yesterday by Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have P2372.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is document that you were shown by Ms. Korner yesterday. It's a criminal report addressed to the high prosecutor in Sarajevo temporarily --

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe this was in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can we have the tab number, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's tab number 5 of the Prosecutor's binder. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The documents gathered in 1992, are they used in criminal proceedings in all these cases?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tusevljak, Ms. Korner showed you a report for the period the 2nd of September, 1992, dated October 1992, and it's a report on -- or, rather, it's a report on the Sarajevo Romanija-Birac CSB. It's P793 and P2375. It's your own administration's report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have P2375. It's Prosecution tab 35.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I would like you to comment on it. On page 22716, Ms. Korner quoted from this document and from the other one, the other report, and she said: Documenting of criminal offences against Serbs is a specific issue. This sector is undertaking great efforts to adequately document those criminal offences despite great difficulties. What great difficulties are you referring to here?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was impossible to go into the field. We did not have evidence collected on site. We did not have medical documentation. As I've already stated, often when the VRS would be involved in a body exchange, very often we were not present. We were not even aware of the exchanges. And at the same time we had a constant lack of professional adequately-trained personnel, because nobody, beginning with me, no member of the crime prevention police had ever encountered this kind of criminal offences in their careers up to date. At that moment we practically knew nothing about it, how to document them, what to do about them, what procedure to follow. That was our greatest problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you undertake any measures in relation to this? Did the Ministry of the Interior undertake any measures in relation to this, such as instructive dispatches, guide-lines, and the like?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We used to receive dispatches from the Ministry of the Interior. We, from the crime prevention police department, also attempted to draw up a sort of a brochure. It was a dispatch with instructions on how crime prevention police should act and what the operative should do. The most experienced forensic technician did the same thing and he also dispatched an instruction on the forensic procedures to be followed in the field. I also believe that towards the end of the year we organised a training for forensic technicians in the RS MUP. The goal of all these measures was to improve the work of the crime prevention police. Among other things, we didn't have properly trained forensic technicians, that is, people who could go on site and document the event using appropriate methods.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At the very end of her cross-examination - and this is going to be my last question as well, my last topic, to be more precise - Ms. Korner spoke about the annual report of the Ministry of the Interior. It's P625. It relates to the period between April and December 1992. It is dated January 1993. It's Prosecution tab pre-1B. Do you remember that you spoke with Ms. Korner about this document? She quoted some passages from this document. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was given this report to read it in my hotel room, and I read it from the first to the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown page, I believe it's 17 in Serbian. The number in the lower right-hand corner should be 13 -- or, rather -- well, actually, yes, 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is the section devoted to the Public Security Service. Under A we see the heading "Prevention and Discovery of Crime."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's at page 12 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you please read the last sentence and then we are going to turn the page.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "It should also be emphasised that among the perpetrators there is a certain number of uniformed persons" --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we turn the page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- "who are mainly members of paramilitary formations, but also army reservists." And then there is a remark saying: "Criminal offences committed by the members of the VRS would normally be referred by the organs of the military police."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No need to read the footnotes.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "And police reservists, while some of the criminals used camouflage uniforms and even the insignia of the Army of Republika Srpska and the police."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, no. Do you also know or do you have any information about similar occurrences?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Very often perpetrators of criminal offences put on the VRS uniform or police uniforms and then proceeded to commit criminal offences.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On the following page, Ms. Korner read the last paragraph, where it says that the most grave forms of crimes that have occurred lately --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we also have it in English. I would like to be able to follow. It should be -- yes, the third paragraph. The third paragraph in English; this is what I'm quoting from.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So: "The most severe forms of crime which appeared in this war period for brutality, ruthlessness, and other elements comprising are the crimes against humanity and international law. The number of these crimes is surely much greater, and the collection of documents is a difficult and long-term work. We have registered 101 crimes against humanity and international law." Mr. Tusevljak, you worked on crime prevention and detection. Do you agree with the contents of this paragraph of this report?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, entirely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Further on, on the page marked with a number 17 which means --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, I'm not sure which page of the Serbian version are we looking at now. Thank you. Can we have the same in English, please. It should be page 15 in English, towards the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Korner read out the claim that the focus of the operative work in the CSB was concentrated on members of the enemy forces who committed crimes and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm interested in page marked with a number 19 which in English could be page 17. So it's 19 in Serbian, 17 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I would like you to comment on it. First, could you please read the second paragraph beginning with the words "during this period."

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In this period, 7.807 criminal reports were filed in the area of general crime" --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, it's page 16 in English, the fourth paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Go on. Excuse me for interrupting you.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In this period, 7.807 criminal reports were filed for common crime. The results are relatively satisfactory, especially if we bear in mind the circumstances in which the crimes were perpetrated" --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just one comment before we go on the break: We find a number of 7.807 criminal reports, do you remember the number of the criminal reports for war crimes and breaches of international law?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this report, 101.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Does this represent a comparatively smaller percentage or - how should I put it? - significantly lesser percentage in relation to the total number of criminal reports filed in the period?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you can see it from the number of the criminal reports filed for common crime and for war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Tusevljak, if some tasks have priority in the MUP, what are the hallmarks of the results of this priority work?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main characteristics is the number of the cases solved. That's the only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see the time, Your Honours. I have perhaps less than ten minutes, but I also have to inform the Trial Chamber about a certain matter, that is why I propose that we go on the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tusevljak, in this report, this annual report, we see on the one hand that the police had the priority to process war crimes. On the other hand, we see the actual number of criminal reports that were filed. Tell me, what is your opinion, why are the numbers as they are?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, first of all, that these are reports that are filed on daily basis by citizens. I think that the public security from Banja Luka has filed the greatest number of reports that were originally instituted by individual citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, you didn't understand me. I'm talking here about the war crimes report. You just told us that 101 criminal reports were filed for war crimes. On the other hand we see in this report that war crimes had the priority. So how can you explain this? What is the reason? How come that something that has been given high priority resulted in a comparatively small number of criminal reports?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the reason for that is the small number of operatives working in the field who were able to deal with war crimes; that's number one. Number two, very often the police were simply unable to act on the reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say "unable to act," are you referring to some objective reasons or some other reasons?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: War resulted in the fact that the police was unable to reach the places where war crimes were committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The 101 criminal report for war crimes, what does it pertain to? Who were the victims in the 101 criminal reports?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe all three ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And finally, could you read the last paragraph on this page. This is the conclusion given by the Ministry of the Interior in relation to the issue of war crimes. Read it and then I'm going to ask you a question.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Despite --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the English version back on the screen. Yes. It begins on this page and then goes on to the following. It's the last paragraph, the last sentence on this page. And then the paragraph continues on the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Go on, Mr. Tusevljak.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In spite of taking and initiating various measures, the documentation of crimes against humanity and international law is not satisfactory. In the MUP, apart from daily instructions and providing direct help to the Security Services Centres and public security stations, decisions by the expert collegium of ministers, issuance of wanted circulars for war criminals (one a day on average) and the like, a special meeting was held with the leaders regarding these issues and detailed questionnaires drawn up to collect data on war criminals and victims of crimes. Co-operation was established with some of the media in order to exchange data and documents, et cetera."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, do you agree with this position of the Ministry of the Interior as it is stated in this report? Do you know anything about such measures being undertaken at the time?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with this position, and I am aware of the measures that were undertaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, Ms. Korner, at the very end of yesterday's examination on page 22737, stated the following - I'll say it in English: [In English] "Mr. Tusevljak, let's final this, because I ought to make it clear to you: I'm suggesting that it's quite clear -- and I'm not suggesting this is what you wanted to happen, but it's quite clear that your clear instructions from your bosses from, I suggest, the minister downwards was to investigate war crimes against Serbs and effectively not to bother with the war crimes that were committed against the non-Serbs? And that's the reality, isn't it?" And your answer: "No. Investigations were conducted in other cases of crimes, not only when it's Serbs?" [Interpretation] Mr. Tusevljak, did you have any sort of instructions from your superiors in the Ministry of the Interior, including anybody from the headquarters of the Ministry of the Interior, including the minister, to investigate only war crimes against Serbs and not to deal with the war crimes committed against non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never received such instructions from anybody in the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, if such instructions had been issued in 1992, would it have been in accordance with the Law on the Interior?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, such an instruction would not be in accordance with the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Bearing this in mind, if members of the Ministry of the Interior had received such an instruction, would they be duty-bound to act upon it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The instructions, contrary to the Law on the Interior, are not the instructions that are binding for the members of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And finally, Mr. Tusevljak, had you received such an instruction, would you have acted upon it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no more questions for this witness. I would just like to remind the Chamber: On page 22456, during examination-in-chief of this witness, I proposed to de-MFI 1D214 to 1D232. 232. Ms. Korner at the time requested that the decision by the Trial Chamber should be postponed until the end of her cross-examination. The cross-examination is finished and I believe that the documents in question were not even mentioned, or at least not in the sense which would present an obstacle for them to be de-MFI'd. Therefore, I propose that the documents 1D214 to 1D232 should be admitted into evidence without being merely marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Could you, on a thumbnail, remind me as to what these documents were, please, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, those are the expert autopsy reports from the CSB Banja Luka which were shown to the witness Tusevljak -- Tutus during his cross-examination in, well, a year ago. And the problem, Your Honour, was that the objection at that point was the authenticity of the documents. And if you remember, I have shown the document -- the receipt of the documents which we received from the -- from the witness here and the RS MUP, and he confirmed that all these documents, which I had shown to him, are the documents which we received from the RS MUP. And therefore the issue of authenticity, in our opinion, does not exist anymore. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I don't have Ms. Korner's specific instructions on this, but I seem to recall the issue was more of the fact that they were forensic documents and they couldn't -- there was no nexus between either Mr. Tutus or this witness for them to be admitted and that authenticity wasn't the one and only hurdle in the way of their admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But inasmuch as Mr. Zecevic has said, the -- Ms. Korner's most recent application was to defer the decision until after her cross-examination had been completed, and she didn't touch it. It appears that it has ceased to be a matter of concern for the Prosecution, notwithstanding -- and I'm not ignoring what you just said, Ms. Pidwell, so for purely practical purposes, for the reasons that Mr. Zecevic gave in response to my question as to what this witness has said about them, it seems that that is the course we should follow. So the MFI qualification on these documents would be removed and they would be entered as full exhibits. Mr. Tusevljak, your examination is now at an end. You are now released as a witness. You are free to go, and we wish you a safe journey back to your home. We thank you for coming to assist the Tribunal and giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So as would have happened over the past few days, we have some procedural matters we wish to deal. We wouldn't be rising immediately, so the usher will escort you from the courtroom. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I suppose we have to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And I suppose there's a way of my -- of Mr. Krgovic's confirmation that -- not Krgovic's confirmation. Well, I will repeat the order of the Chamber, the direction of the Chamber, that the previous direction to Mr. Krgovic that the Zupljanin Defence begin on the 11th of July is rescinded and we will now take the adjournment, in the current case, to Monday, the 4th of July. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 4th day of July, 2011, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.03 p.m.,
